BreakingNewsTab.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to resume Ukraine peace talks
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.

Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.

The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.

Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."

The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.

It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.

Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.

"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.

Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."

The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.

Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.

Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".

Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.

US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.

Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.

Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.

When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.

"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
BreakingNewsTab.text:
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?

"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.

In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.

But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.

The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.

In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."

For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.

Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".

The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.

"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.

Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.

"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."

All rather vague.

It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.

He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.

He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.

He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.

The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court.

The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter them if they are already behind bars.

"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.

"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences", she added.

The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer.

Judges will also being able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing.

For criminals aged 18-20, judges will be able to impose similar restrictions but for shorter periods of time, the MoJ said.

However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.

But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".

The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws.

All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.

Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.

Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".

She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.

It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.

Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART.

"We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC.

"My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life.

"But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."

Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something".

"Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families.

"That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said.

The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy.

This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial.

If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease.

The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts.

Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London.

"For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC.

"We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease."

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK's gaps in Arctic defence leave it open to Russian attacks, committee says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK has "glaring gaps" in its ability to defend the Arctic region, leaving it vulnerable to potential Russian attacks, a report by MPs has warned.

The Commons Defence Committee said a shortage of Royal Navy warships and submarines was leaving the country's critical infrastructure in the High North, including undersea cables and energy supplies, exposed.

In the event of a conflict, the report added that Russia could threaten the UK's population, civilian and military infrastructure and vital supply routes across the Atlantic from the US.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said it is "clear-eyed about the threat Russia posed" and is investing heavily to protect Britain's undersea cables.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer previously warned that Russia could attack Nato by the end of the decade.

The High North - which includes the Arctic circle and areas adjacent to it - has become central to the UK's defence concerns in recent years.

Earlier this year, the MoD said Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic is now back to the same levels as the Cold War era.

In the new report, MPs highlighted a "shockingly low availability" of submarines and said there was a temporary loss in ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening Nato sea lanes, UK critical infrastructure and the UK's nuclear deterrent," it added.

Chair of the Defence Committee, Tan Dhesi, said: "This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage."

The work to address these gaps "cannot start soon enough," he added.

In light of uncertainty over US support for Nato, the report said the UK should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on the High North.

An MoD spokesperson said the Jef was already "strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats".

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: "If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

"To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it's too late".

BreakingNewsTab.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
BreakingNewsTab.text:
After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.

Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.

A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.

It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?

It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.

"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.

"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."

On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.

The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.

"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.

It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.

It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.

The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.

Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.

The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.

I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.

Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.

It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.

While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.

UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.

Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.

Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

BreakingNewsTab.title: The real reasons US politicians are getting older
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives.

The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump.

Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s.

Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states.

The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed.

The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population.

At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it?

Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.

Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.

When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.

The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.

Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.

Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.

Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.

The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.

In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington

But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively.

The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39.

There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.

So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her.

Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too.

The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%.

Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast.

Campaigners argue that these demographic trends matter because they leave some issues underrepresented.

"Yes, that might result in older people being elected, but I think it really skews, too, what issues are important; what issues politicians are incentivised to talk about and to take care of," says Grace Mausser, the co-chair of the New York City wing of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Mausser campaigned for Zohran Mamdani in his winning bid last year to become, at age 34, New York City's youngest mayor since 1892. Mamdani was held up as an example of a rare youthful success story, but his ally Mausser is less concerned with a politician's age than with their outlook.

Mausser says it is not necessarily a problem if someone has been in politics for a long time. Rather, the problem can be what may result from that: "You become so used to the language and the ideas of the political establishment that anything else - any new ideas, whether they come from young people or old people - seem crazy."

She invokes left-wing Democratic senator Bernie Sanders, 85, as an example of an older politician with a long tenure on Capitol Hill who has embraced change and had ideas that have resonated across generations.

In the US, older people hold politicians in far higher esteem than younger people - even more so than in many other countries, according to a Pew survey from spring 2025. Some 62% of 18-34-year-olds were likely to say few or none of their elected officials are honest, compared with 45% of people aged over 50. Of the 25 countries surveyed by Pew, only Greece's young adults had a more pessimistic view of the honesty of politicians.

For one expert who studies political engagement on both sides of the Atlantic, disaffection among young people helps to explain their unwillingness to participate in politics. The issue is not helped by the fact Congress has minimum age requirements for members, he says. Candidates must be 30 to serve as a senator, and 25 to be a representative.

"The one leads to another," remarks James Sloam from Royal Holloway, University of London. "If you don't have enough young people engaged in politics generally, then they won't become representatives."

What is more, Sloam says, young people in the US and the UK alike are alert to the fact that power does not just lie in politics. They are aware there are many other areas of work in which they can wield influence - including over elected officials.

For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs.

Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary."

Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave.

JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids."

America's two-party system is cited as another barrier to young people getting involved with politics.

Sloam, the London academic, says this is because only a relatively narrow range of views are represented. He highlights research that indicates young people are more energised by social movements or issue-based campaigns than by party politics.

And within party politics, he notes the example of Mamdani and others on the political left who appear to be galvanising youth support outside the Democratic Party mainstream. But he cautions that "it's a little bit sporadic at the moment".

The Republican Party has been through its own splintering over the last decade with the advent of Trump's MAGA movement, which appealed to a swathe of young men in the 2024 presidential election.

Some European democracies show a more pluralistic political environment can increase youth engagement, Sloam says. Scandinavian countries, for example, which are more likely to be multi-party, provide a clear counter example because the parties of government in those countries "work with those social movements to try and bring them into the political systems". Citing countries such as Norway, Sloam suggests there is a cycle whereby stronger youth turnout and youth trust in the political system leads to more involvement in politics.

Owen, the Republican, fancies his chances in Utah, despite his opponent's much larger war chest.

Discussing what energises him as a Gen Z candidate, he identifies issues including the role of tech in public life, immigration and cost-of-living concerns. "I'm on the front end of starting my own family and looking at the costs and [asking] how am I going to make it work?" he says.

Asked if he sees any similarities between his campaign and the campaigns of young political candidates on the opposite side of the political spectrum, he says: "I'd break down the 'us versus them' framework, and maybe discard that a little bit… [there is] a bipartisan message that a lot of Americans on both sides of the aisle are feeling: that Washington isn't working for them."

He takes a similar view to Mausser, the democratic socialist in New York, that voters should not necessarily pick a candidate because they are young: what matters is their ideas.

"For me, it's much more about what you support, what you're who you're fighting for, than what year you were born," she says.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.

The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.

A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.

The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".

Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.

The shortlisted cities are:

What is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.

What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."

She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."

What is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.

What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".

Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.

A Cambridge study found that of the 86 scientists named by UK exam boards, the English chemist, whose work in the 1950s helped reveal the structure of DNA, was the only woman.

Exam specifications set out the skills and knowledge students are expected to have gained by the end of their course and how they will be assessed.

Exam boards said there was "a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications".

Academics from the University of Cambridge, along with institutions in the US and Australia, examined how many women were mentioned in specifications for biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, geology and astronomy.

Their work, published in the British Educational Research Journal, looked at six exam boards in the UK:

At Key Stage 4 and equivalent, including GCSEs and National 5s in Scotland, Franklin was the only woman among the 86 scientists mentioned.

She was also one of three women mentioned at Key Stage 5 and equivalent - including A-levels, AS-levels, National Highers and National Advanced Highers - out of a total of 181 scientists.

Marie Tharp, an American cartographer who created the first map of the floor of the Atlantic ocean in the 1950s, and Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist who discovered the existence of the Earth's inner core in the 1930s, both feature in the Cambridge OCR's A-­level Geology.

Franklin, who was named in Cambridge OCR's GCSE Biology and Scottish Highers Biology, produced a famous DNA image known as Photograph 51.

Cambridge scientists Francis Crick and James Watson used the image to work out the following year that DNA has a double-helix structure.

Watson, Crick and Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Franklin had died four years earlier.

Academics who wrote the paper found that "several major scientific breakthroughs" in specifications were made by women, but they were not explicitly mentioned.

The paper said: "Many of the scientific discoveries and explanations were developed in the 1800s and early 1900s, a period when scientific and mathematical practice was largely, but not solely, dominated by men.

"Our findings confirm that the UK science specifications reflect this historical imbalance: although women made significant contributions to major scientific breakthroughs, this fact is rarely acknowledged."

The academics recommended that Franklin should be included "in all specifications when teaching DNA structure".

They also said specifications should refer to Marie Curie, who discovered radium and polonium and coined the term radioactivity, and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner, who discovered nuclear fission, among others.

Stephanie Buttigieg, one of the authors, said: "Relatable role models can help keep more girls in STEM by strengthening their sense of belonging in science and fostering positive attitudes towards scientific careers."

A spokeswoman for the Joint Council for Qualifications, which represents AQA, Cambridge OCR, CCEA, WJEC and Pearson, said: "Exam boards recognise that there is a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications, and this is an area they will be focusing on as these qualifications are reformed."

Qualifications Scotland said the Curriculum Improvement Cycle offered "an opportunity to consider gender representation within our future qualifications and assessments".

The Department for Education in England said "girls should see the contribution women have made in STEM", adding it was "committed to improving the school curriculum over the coming years, and as part of that will make sure every girl can see where their learning can take them".

The Scottish Government said it was "committed to closing the gender gap in STEM and will carefully consider the findings of this research".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.

Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.

"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.

The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.

It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.

The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.

The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.

He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".

Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.

On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".

The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.

Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.

He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.

The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere.

At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined.

Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment.

"And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".

A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles.

Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected."

Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all."

The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up.

But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair".

His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence.

In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin.

She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."

Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.''

The trial continues.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain
BreakingNewsTab.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.

Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.

Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".

It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.

Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.

Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.

Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.

The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.

Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...

"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."

On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".

He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.

"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."

"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.

Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.

The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.

It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.

While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.

Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

FinanceTab.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
FinanceTab.text:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.

She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".

"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.

The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.

She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.

"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.

The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".

He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".

Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.

"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.

He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."

Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.

But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

FinanceTab.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
FinanceTab.text:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

FinanceTab.title: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad
FinanceTab.text:
Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place.

"I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."

More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey, external of 15,000 final year university students.

Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high.

UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report, external.

For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?

Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for insurance giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.

She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.

Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched.

"People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."

Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.

West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching.

"I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live.

"In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."

This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.

Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020.

"Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."

Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon.

"To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."

Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.

"When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."

Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London.

"I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."

FinanceTab.title: Inflation and borrowing data illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
FinanceTab.text:
The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.

From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.

The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.

The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.

Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.

These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.

On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.

While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.

The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.

The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.

FinanceTab.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
FinanceTab.text:
UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week.

The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts.

Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules.

Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September. It is the highest inflation has been since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

September's inflation figure is also important because it suggests how benefits will increase next April.

It means the state pension will most likely rise by 3.9%, in line with average wage rises from May to July, due to the triple lock.

The inflation figure for September also dictates how other benefits will rise in April. By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

FinanceTab.title: Andy Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
FinanceTab.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.

These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.

Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.

But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use.

This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.

Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.

FinanceTab.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
FinanceTab.text:
The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year.

Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are:

In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk.

Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. While a rise in government borrowing costs will increase debt interest payments, higher inflation could push up tax revenues.

KPMG believes the government's buffer could have fallen to £12bn, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates it could be £20bn.

There has been speculation over what specific measures will be announced in the Budget.

Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets.

Your First Home scheme

Further details on the Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget.

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

There had been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. However, this has now been ruled out.

The Times has reported, external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms.

The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

Healey told the BBC in late September that the time and place for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again.

Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276.

There has been speculation, external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits.

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the mansion tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028.

FinanceTab.title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
FinanceTab.text:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".

A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.

FinanceTab.title: Google says cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites resolved
FinanceTab.text:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase.

Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money.

"Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC.

"This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time."

She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions.

"It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added.

More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday.

A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage.

"We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout.

"We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services.

A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon".

Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hours during an outage at AWS' largest cloud site.

Experts say this latest outage show how many businesses still rely on core services provided by a few large cloud operators.

"Google Cloud's outage is a reminder of how deeply our economies depend on just a handful of cloud providers," said Prof Feng Li, associate dean for research & innovation at Bayes Business School.

He added that it was not yet clear what caused the power problem identified by Google Cloud.

"Large cloud systems are complex, and failures will happen.

"What matters is how far they spread, how quickly services recover and whether customers have workable alternatives," he added.
