articles.title: Angel Reese stars again as Atlanta Dream thrash Valkyries to seize WNBA finals lead
articles.text:
Angel Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 on Wednesday night and take a 2-1 lead in the WNBA finals.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who host Game 4 on Saturday.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for their first victory in the finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the finals.

“It feels good when you’re in the finals. It’s a long season and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the offseason is for,” Reese said. “I put the work in for this moment and I’m just happy I could lead the team to a win. We’re feeling good going into Saturday.”

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes’ layup, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter by scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

Atlanta have dominated the third quarter so far in the series, outscoring Golden State 63-35 across the three games.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who was fouled.

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

This game was originally scheduled to be played on Thursday at the Gateway Center Arena, where the Dream play most of their home games. The league was able to work with the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena to play the next two games of the championship series there so that they could have a much bigger crowd. Gateway seats only 3,500. State Farm Arena can seat more than 17,000 fans.

“Protect home court,” Howard said of the team’s focus. “Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It’s big. We went and stole one but we can’t let them come in and do the same thing.”

Wednesday night’s game was sold out, as is Game 4 on Saturday, which will also be played at State Farm Arena. The crowd included several music stars, including Ludacris and 2 Chainz, as well as actor Kerry Washington.

Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom said he was going to be at the game. The Atlanta Dream and State Farm Arena offered him a private suite for his protection. He refused to sit in it and was removed from the game.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed their first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket for the Valkyries with 4:39 left. They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive three-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

The hot three-point shooting continued in the second quarter as Atlanta built their lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State were able to hang around and trailed only 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48%) from behind the arc. That was more made three-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Reese had 15 points and WNBA sixth woman of the year Janelle Salaun had 11 for the Valkyries.

Games 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million viewers, the most ever to watch the first game of the finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

articles.title: Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penalty
articles.text:
It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.

Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged.

Enter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League games; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday. He now has 16 goals against Arsenal; he has only scored more against one club – Leicester, against whom he has 20.

Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. That would have been too much because Bayern shaded an absorbing tie in terms of clear chances created. But Arsenal made their point. They were value for it.

Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not previously lost a Champions League group or league phase match at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws. Arteta’s players were not intimidated. They bristled with assurance at the outset and Rice rewarded their never-say-die spirit. Bayern had wanted revenge for their 3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadium in the league stage last season. They did not get it.

Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his lineup. He made just two changes, Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.

Was it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was a substitute. He came on in the 68th minute only to be forced off before the end. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.

Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.

It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.

Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, although his teammate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through ball for Davies which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.

Bayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.

It is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and songs from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.

The pre-game surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Rice’s corner only for Neuer to produce an extraordinary save.

The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks against Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.

It was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see that Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into the right-hand corner.

Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who produced the sucker punch. Eze was dangerous throughout. And when the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake.

articles.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued
articles.text:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.

The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.

"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.

Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.

And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.

Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.

They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.

Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance, external" without specifying the reason.

The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz.

Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet.

Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.

OpenAI said in a blog post, external that the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.

The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered.

"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.

It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.

While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.

It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.

The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.

Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.

"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.

Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning, external.

"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.

Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.

The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.

"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.

He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".

The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".

Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.

Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was, external "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".

The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".

It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.

The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.

PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.

Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
articles.text:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".

Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.

Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.

Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.

They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.

"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday.

"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."

The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.

Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.

He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.

Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.

While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.

It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.

New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.

The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".

As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.

Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people.

"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.

To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.

The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.

Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.

Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock.

Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?
articles.text:
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.

Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.

Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.

During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield."

Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things.

Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.

Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.

Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.

The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.

Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle".

Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.

Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.

He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.

But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.

"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.

SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%.

Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.

In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.

Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.

Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.

However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.

Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.

"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.

The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed...

articles.title: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.text:
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.

The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.

Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.

A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.

The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.

Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.

Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.

articles.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
articles.text:
For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.

But that may end soon.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.

Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.

"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.

BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.

Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.

But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.

Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.

While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.

Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.

Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.

While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".

Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.

The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.

Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.

Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."

While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

articles.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
articles.text:
Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the suspect's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who police say then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

DNA science isn't the only technology that is helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major investigations like the hunt for Sperino's attacker is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating her murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
articles.text:
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.

A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.

Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.

The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.

District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".

"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.

The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.

In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.

However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.

The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.

The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".

Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.

articles.title: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech
articles.text:
UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower".

It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall.

Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation.

Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK.

In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets.

"This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards".

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals.

However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches.

The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
articles.text:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial.

The Saudi government did not respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: DeepSeek banned from US government in race with China for AI dominance
articles.text:
The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models.

As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race.

While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China.

The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment.

The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.

The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded.

The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms.

White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China.

Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek.

US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country.

DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times.

While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers.

Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek.

For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would.

Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own.

Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling.

The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding.

articles.title: Uber wins bid to throw out £340m lawsuits from black cab drivers
articles.text:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.

The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.

But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.

Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.

About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.

The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.

In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.

RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.

Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.

The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

articles.title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
articles.text:
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.

The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."

The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what has been causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.

"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.

In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.

During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.

Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.

"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.

"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."

Misdiagnoses can be extremely distressing for people dealing with chronic illnesses, said Dr Michael Kornberg.

"It becomes part of your identity," the associate professor of neurology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine said, noting how there is a "comfort" in knowing what is happening inside your body.

"To live with that for five years and then to be given a different diagnosis is really unsettling."

Dr Marwa Kaisey, a guest on Tuesday's episode, said MS misdiagnoses are not uncommon because symptoms are inconsistent and there is no universal testing.

"It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says 'yes, you have it. No, you don't,'" Kaisey said. "It's a list of criteria."

About 15 to 20 percent of patients diagnosed with MS do not actually have the disease, research suggests, according to Elena Grebenciucova, a neuroimmunology physician at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago.

Dr Grebenciucova said the illness is typically diagnosed by finding a number of lesions - or white matter spots - with an MRI of the brain or spinal cord.

But she said those white matter spots can sometimes be signs of different health problems or illnesses, like migraines, high blood pressure, high blood sugar and high cholesterol.

The neurology doctor said another health condition, a vitamin B12 deficiency, can also lead to neurological problems that closely mirror MS symptoms, including cognitive decline, tingling and balance issues.

MS is a diagnosis of exclusion, with doctors combing through a patient's medical history and many laboratory tests to make a determination, explained Dr Philip De Jager, the director of the Multiple Sclerosis Center at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

Because misdiagnoses can happen, Dr De Jager said that patients should seek second opinions.

Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in August 2021, after experiencing symptoms for a while, saying at the time: "It's been a tough road. But as we all know, the road keeps on going."

Years later, she described being in a "real depression" and said in a 2024 episode of her podcast that "I don't enjoy living. I don't enjoy it. I don't enjoy things anymore".

She had said in a New York Times interview that she could not walk without a cane and used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix series Dead To Me.

articles.title: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+
articles.text:
We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.

Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.

The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.

The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.

The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.

In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.

Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.

The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.

In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.

Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.

On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again".

"I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said.

Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think so… It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break.

"I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."

In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.

He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members".

"It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see."

He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it."

It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return.

"I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes."

Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera, who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez.

"It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school.

"But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it."

Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning.

Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.

Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges.

A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside.

Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars.

articles.title: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?
articles.text:
"This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.

Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.

Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.

The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.

But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character.

Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments.

Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return.

And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community".

Baron Cohen acknowledged an inevitable backlash when he first announced the sequel, writing on X: "In an age where a comedian's career can be ended by a single un-PC joke, I thought I'd play it safe and bring this guy back."

Recently, he shared a video, external posted to a newly created Instagram account, in which a grey-haired academic urged viewers to boycott the upcoming film. The character appeared to be Baron Cohen in prosthetic make-up.

Has Ali G passed his sell-by date? Or are racial stereotypes, and those who believe them, the true butt of the joke?

Alternatively, as some critics argue, is the whole thing simply not very funny?

The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.

But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.

Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls.

"Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."

Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities".

When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant".

"Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent.

"I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."

Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations.

Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview.

"I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."

When discussing the forthcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".

In a new essay in Time this week, external, Baron Cohen argued that his characters have always been "vehicles to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity", and that in the case of Ali G, "the joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment" he aims to expose.

"The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him," Baron Cohen wrote.

"The world he's returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven't just lingered - they've metastasized. They're fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history - social media - and now by its monstrous child, AI."

One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.

"It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media.

While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago.

"This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."

It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

articles.title: Author Helen Fielding launches award to find the next Bridget Jones's Diary
articles.text:
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a new prize aimed at discovering funny diary writers from the north of England, saying opportunities across the UK are "very uneven".

West Yorkshire-born Fielding, who penned Bridget's famous diary as well co-writing the film adaptations, has set up the Bridget Jones Prize, external with charity New Writing North.

The award will go to the person who submits the funniest 1,000-word piece of first-person writing.

Speaking at an event for the Independent, which first published Bridget's diary in 1995, Fielding said the spread of opportunity for writing in the UK is "very uneven", adding: "There's much more opportunity in the south than in the north, where I grew up."

The winner of the new prize - set to run for an initial three years from 2027 to 2029 - will receive a £2,000 prize and a package of writing support from Fielding's literary agents and New Writing North.

Fielding's original newspaper column went on to be published as a best-selling novel titled Bridget Jones's Diary in 1996.

It spawned several sequels and hit movie adaptations starring Renée Zellweger as the endearingly chaotic and lovelorn thirty-something diarist.

articles.title: Woman told Russell Brand he 'treated her like an animal', court hears
articles.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

One of the women who claims Russell Brand raped her later told him he had "treated her like an animal", a court has heard.

The comedian's trial at Southwark Crown Court in London has been hearing recorded police interviews with a female complainant, who claims she did not consent to anal sex with him at his house in 2009.

Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. He has said he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

On Wednesday, the jury heard an interview with a woman who says she first met Brand at one of his comedy shows at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

She said she had a boyfriend at the time but went to his dressing room, where she performed a sex act on him.

The woman said it was during their next meeting at his house when the sex was not consensual and she had only agreed to vaginal sex.

Asked by the detective in the interview whether there was ever a conversation about anal sex, she replied: "No."

She said she was surprised to receive a "random" text message from Brand six months later, saying he wanted to "push her further".

She said she replied asking: "Why are you even messaging me?"

"I remember his response, saying, 'Because you're dirty and I want to push you further'."

The jury heard that the woman did not respond straight away because she was upset, but then replied saying: "I think you've pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal."

The woman added: "I do remember his response was immediate. He said, 'I'm sorry'."

During cross-examination, the woman was asked by defence barrister Ian Winter KC about her decision to meet Brand.

"You made it clear that you went to his house to have sex with him, knowing his reputation," he said.

She said that was "correct", adding: "I want to flag that I wanted to go there, I take ownership."

The woman said she had a couple of glasses of alcohol while getting ready at home and another glass while waiting in a restaurant for Brand's driver to pick her up on the day of the alleged rape.

The court heard he made her shower and brush her teeth before they had sex.

Winter suggested that Brand asked her to do so because he did not like the smell of alcohol "because of his soberism", but the woman said it was because "he didn't like the smell of my hair".

When questioning her about the alleged rape, Winter put to the female complainant: "You had vaginal sex with a condom on and then it finished with you agreeing to anal sex."

The woman replied: "I did not consent to that at that time.

"We're not here to discuss my morality. We're here to discuss criminality. I thought I was going to have penetrative vaginal sex.

"He acted like nothing happened."

She broke down in tears at the end of giving her evidence.

The trial continues.

articles.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027 coach tickets oversold in admin error
articles.text:
An administrative error resulted in coach journeys to the Glastonbury Festival being oversold through its official ticketing partner.

More coach package tickets were sold for certain departures than there are seats available, according to an email See Tickets sent to customers.

Those affected will not lose their tickets however. Instead, their booking will automatically be converted into a general admission ticket and the coach fare will be refunded.

The ticketing agency declined to comment further, but the BBC understands Glastonbury Festival was not responsible for the error.

Glastonbury coach ticket prices range from £26 to £185 - on top of general admission - depending on the departure town or city and whether it is a single or return journey.

Affected customers have been told that unless they opt to keep their coach seat by 31 October 2026, their booking will automatically be converted to general admission.

The coach fare will then be refunded to the card used for the original booking.

See Tickets' customer services department assured customers the error will not affect festival deposits, and ticket holders will be able to pay the remaining balance for their tickets as normal in April.

The agency apologised and thanked customers for their understanding, adding: "We're looking forward to welcoming you to the festival in June."

articles.title: Belfast comedian Vittorio Angelone criticised for rape "joke"
articles.text:
A Belfast comedian has been criticised for making a rape "joke" about a woman who had recently spoken publicly about being the victim of a sexual assault.

Vittorio Angelone, who has since apologised on social media, referred to content creator Rebecca Goodwin in a remark about rape which he made in a podcast episode in 2025.

Goodwin, who had previously reported a rape to police, said it will "forever live with me that it was allowed for my name to be used as the punchline of a malicious 'joke' about such a serious issue".

Angelone said he has reached out to Goodwin and apologised directly.

Goodwin had claimed that Angelone posted videos of the "joke" on his social media accounts in recent days.

Rape Crisis Northern Ireland and Dublin Rape Crisis Centre have both criticised the remarks.

The makers of the podcast have been contacted for comment.

During a 2025 episode of the 'Have a Word' podcast, Angelone asked of fellow comedian Freddy Quinne "if you're here, who's raping Rebecca Goodwin?".

British OnlyFans creator Rebecca Goodwin had previously spoken publicly about being the victim of sexual assault.

The comments were made during a "roast" episode of the podcast posted in December 2025.

The episode, which Goodwin was not involved in, contained comedians taking turns insulting each other in front of an audience.

In a post on Facebook, Goodwin said the episode was recorded "in September/October of 2025 and has been behind a paywall for a year before being published to social media".

She reported a rape to police in July 2025 and had spoken publicly about her experience.

Goodwin said she only became aware of the comments when clips were posted to social media in recent days.

"I am grateful I never saw it sooner because it would've been just weeks after [the assault] happened and I was in a different mental state to what I am now," she said.

At that time, Goodwin said that "no contact or apology has been attempted" by Angelone, but that he had "removed the joke from his own social media, again, over a year after it was made, edited, clipped, captioned and posted with my full name included".

The comments have not been edited out of the paywalled episode of the podcast.

Goodwin said: "We are facing a global crisis of violence against women and girls, and we are begging for our safety and experiences to be taken seriously."

She added that Freddy Quinne, as well as a number of other comedians who were part of the podcast episode, had since apologised to her.

However, Goodwin said that she did not accept the apologies as they "only came a year after the joke was made and nobody had my back in that room at the time, up until I made a social media post about it".

Quinne has been approached for comment.

In a statement on Instagram, Angelone said he let his "need for validation supersede my own standards and morals".

"It's completely pathetic and I'm ashamed to realise that about myself," he said.

Angelone will feature in his first major acting role in upcoming BBC sitcom Rewarding, which is set to air this autumn.

A BBC spokesperson said: "We are aware of the concerns that have been raised and are actively considering them, recognising their seriousness and the sensitivities involved."

Rape Crisis Northern Ireland said they were "very disappointed to hear of the comments made by Vittorio Angelone which contribute to a culture in which rape and sexual violence can be trivialised".

"When rape becomes a punchline and sexual violence is treated as entertainment, it becomes easier to dismiss its impact and harder for survivors to speak out."

It continued: "Those with a public platform and an audience have a responsibility to consider the impact of the language they use and the attitudes they help to normalise.

"Rape jokes might seem far removed from an act of sexual violence, but they sit within that same culture of minimising and trivialising it."

They added "survivors should never be left feeling that what happened to them is something that could be laughed at, minimised or dismissed".

Chief Executive of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, Rachel Morrogh, said: "For survivors, hearing rape treated as a punchline can be deeply hurtful, and it reinforces the attitudes that discourage people from coming forward.

"Anyone with a public platform, including performers, promoters and venues, has a responsibility to consider who is listening and the harm this kind of material can do. To treat sexual violence as a joke betrays a deep lack of understanding of what survivors have lived through."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
